title: Artificial intelligence in digital pathology: Principles, applications, challenges, and future directions

sections.title: 研究问题
sections.text:
《Artificial intelligence in digital pathology: Principles, applications, challenges, and future directions》：研究问题的原文依据。

【Whole-slide imaging · p0050】The imaging modality used during slide acquisition depends on the specimen type and staining protocol. Brightfield imaging is the standard approach for routine histopathology, including H&E, IHC, and special stains. In brightfield scanning, transmitted light passes through the tissue section to capture morphological and architectural details. Most clinical WSI systems scan brightfield slides at 20× or 40× objective magnification.10

【Whole-slide imaging · p0055】In contrast, fluorescence imaging is used for applications such as fluorescence in situ hybridization, multiplex immunofluorescence, and quantitative biomarker analysis. Fluorescence scanners excite fluorophore-labeled targets with specific wavelengths of light and detect the emitted light, enabling visualization of nucleic acids, proteins, and other molecular markers.11 Similar objective magnifications (typically 20×–40×) are employed. Researchers have developed dual-mode scanners, including the Aperio FL,12 OptraSCAN OS-FLi,13 and SLIDEVIEW VS200,14 which integrate both brightfield and fluorescence imaging within a single platform, allowing labs to image multiple specimen types at the same time.

Fluorescence scanners excite fluorophore-labeled targets with specific wavelengths of light and detect the emitted light, enabling visualization of nucleic acids, proteins, and other molecular markers.11 Similar objective magnifications (typically 20×–40×) are employed. Researchers have developed dual-mode scanners, including the Aperio FL,12 OptraSCAN OS-FLi,13 and SLIDEVIEW VS200,14 which integrate both brightfield and fluorescence imaging within a single platform, allowing labs to image multiple specimen types at the same time.

sections.title: 研究方法
sections.text:
《Artificial intelligence in digital pathology: Principles, applications, challenges, and future directions》：方法与研究设计的原文依据。

【Current implementation in US medical centers · p0205】To ensure reliable implementation, professional organizations have established technical and operational recommendations for WSI systems. The College of American Pathologists (CAP) recommends that scanners support features such as high-throughput image acquisition, appropriate scanning magnification, Z-stacking, and extended depth of field imaging when clinically indicated.50 In addition, labs operating under the Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments (CLIA) must ensure that digital pathology workflows meet established standards for personnel qualifications, test validation, quality control, and quality assurance.51 In the USA, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) also plays an important role in the implementation of digital pathology through oversight of CLIA.52 CMS requires labs performing digital pathology for patient care to comply with CLIA regulations. In 2023, new Current Procedural Terminology codes for digital pathology image acquisition and digitization became effective, providing a standardized mechanism for reporting WSI scanning services.

【Current implementation in US medical centers · p0190】Since the introduction of WSI technology in the early 2000s, digital pathology has evolved rapidly through advances in scanner hardware, IMSs, and AI. Successive generations of WSI scanners have demonstrated substantial improvements in scan speed, throughput, image quality, slide capacity, and workflow efficiency.45

sections.title: 主要结果
sections.text:
《Artificial intelligence in digital pathology: Principles, applications, challenges, and future directions》：结果的原文依据；数值与适用人群以引文为准。

【Generalizability, domain shift, and external validation · p0260】A major challenge for AI in digital pathology is generalizability, defined as the ability of a model to maintain its performance when applied to data from institutions or clinical settings that differ from those represented in the training dataset. Domain shift occurs when the distribution of deployment data differs systematically from that of the training data. In digital pathology, such differences may arise from variations in staining protocols, tissue fixation and processing, section thickness, scanners, imaging settings, magnification, specimen preparation, or patient populations.60

【Generalizability, domain shift, and external validation · p0265】These technical and clinical differences can introduce institution- or batch-specific features that AI models may inadvertently learn instead of disease-relevant morphological characteristics.61 This problem can be particularly pronounced when technical characteristics are correlated with disease labels or patient populations in the training dataset. As a result, a model may demonstrate strong performance during internal validation but experience a decline in performance when evaluated on data from another institution with different data-generating conditions.

【Current implementation in US medical centers · p0190】Since the introduction of WSI technology in the early 2000s, digital pathology has evolved rapidly through advances in scanner hardware, IMSs, and AI. Successive generations of WSI scanners have demonstrated substantial improvements in scan speed, throughput, image quality, slide capacity, and workflow efficiency.45

【Current implementation in US medical centers · p0195】More specifically in the USA, a major milestone occurred in 2017, when the US FDA approved the Philips IntelliSite Pathology Solution as the first WSI system for primary diagnosis.46 This approval enabled pathologists to review and interpret digitized histopathological slides instead of relying exclusively on conventional light microscopy, paving the way for broader clinical adoption of digital pathology.
